The Complete Split AC System

Two units work as one system: the indoor unit cools the room air and the outdoor unit releases the heat outside. Copper pipes, a power cable and a drain pipe connect them.

  1. Hangs on the wall inside the room. It pulls in warm room air, cools it over the evaporator coil and blows it back.

    Why it matters It holds the filters, coil, blower and controls — the parts cleaned during routine servicing.

  2. Sits outside. The compressor and condenser release the heat taken out of your room.

    Why it matters It needs open space around it so the hot air can escape.

  3. Two insulated copper lines carry refrigerant between the units in a closed loop.

    Why it matters Leaks at the joints are the main reason an AC needs gas refilling.

  4. The interconnect cable carries power and control signals between the units.

    Why it matters The AC needs a dedicated, properly earthed supply.

  5. Carries the water removed from the air out of the room.

    Why it matters It must slope downward all the way, or water drips indoors.

Indoor AC Unit Components

Select a part to see what it does. Layouts differ slightly between brands and models.

  1. Closes the unit over the filters and lifts open for cleaning.

    Why it matters Lift it to reach the filters — that is how you clean them at home.

  2. Mesh filters trap dust before it reaches the coil. Clean them every 2–4 weeks.

    Why it matters Clogged filters cut airflow and raise power use; cleaning them is the easiest maintenance.

  3. Copper tubes with aluminium fins. Cold refrigerant evaporates inside and absorbs heat from the room air.

    Why it matters Dust on the coil reduces cooling and causes bad smells; it is cleaned during AC servicing.

  4. A long tangential wheel that pulls room air through the coil and spreads it evenly.

    Why it matters Dust build-up on the blades makes the airflow weak and noisy.

  5. Drives the blower at Low, Medium, High or Auto speed.

    Why it matters If the indoor fan does not run, the room will not cool even when the outdoor unit works.

  6. Sits under the coil and collects the water condensed out of humid air.

    Why it matters A blocked pan or drain is the usual reason for water dripping from the indoor unit.

  7. Carries the condensate out of the room on a continuous downward slope.

    Why it matters A sag or kink in the hose causes water leakage.

  8. Thermistors read the room and coil temperature so the AC knows when to cool, slow down or stop.

    Why it matters A faulty sensor can make the AC stop too early or run without stopping.

  9. The indoor brain: reads the remote and sensors, runs the fan, louver and display, and talks to the outdoor unit.

    Why it matters Power surges and moisture can damage it; error codes on the display often point here.

  10. Shows the set temperature and mode, and holds the remote's infrared receiver.

    Why it matters If the remote stops working, check the batteries and this receiver first.

  11. A small stepper motor swings the louver to aim the cool air up, down or across the room.

    Why it matters Aim the louver to spread cool air across the room rather than straight at people.

  12. The rear chassis carries every internal part and hooks onto the wall-mounting plate.

    Why it matters It must hang level on the wall plate so water drains correctly.

Outdoor AC Unit Components

The outdoor unit holds the compressor and condenser. Layouts differ between brands, and inverter and non-inverter models use different control parts.

  1. Weather-resistant steel base and frame; a partition separates the fan side from the compressor side.

    Why it matters Keep it clear of leaves and debris so air can flow freely.

  2. The heart of the system: it compresses refrigerant gas, raising its pressure and temperature.

    Why it matters Inverter ACs vary the compressor speed to save power; non-inverter models switch it on and off.

  3. Hot refrigerant releases your room's heat to the outside air here and condenses back to liquid.

    Why it matters Dirty fins make the AC work harder; washing them during service improves cooling.

  4. Pulls outside air through the condenser coil to carry the heat away.

    Why it matters If this fan stops, the heat cannot leave and the AC cools poorly or trips.

  5. Drives the propeller fan from a bracket in the fan compartment.

    Why it matters Worn bearings make a grinding noise — an early sign it needs attention.

  6. Controls the compressor and fan; in inverter models it also varies the compressor speed.

    Why it matters Inverter models use an inverter drive board here; non-inverter models use simpler relay controls.

  7. Helps start and run the compressor and fan motors, mainly in non-inverter models.

    Why it matters In non-inverter models, a weak capacitor is a common reason the outdoor unit hums but does not start.

  8. Brass valves where the copper pipes connect; used for vacuuming, gas charging and isolation.

    Why it matters Gas pressure is checked here, and leaks are often found at the flare joints.

  9. Where the interconnect cable from the indoor unit and the power supply are terminated.

    Why it matters Loose or burnt terminals cause tripping; connections must be tight and correctly earthed.

  10. Guards the fan blades while letting air flow freely.

    Why it matters Never run the unit without it, and keep fingers and objects away from the fan.

Layouts differ between brands and models; this is a typical split-AC outdoor unit.

Split AC Installation

A correct installation keeps the AC efficient, quiet and leak-free. These are the key steps a trained technician follows.

  1. Fixed level on a solid wall, with clearance above and at the sides.

    Why it matters A crooked plate makes water collect and leak from one side.

  2. A hole of about 65 mm, drilled sloping slightly down to the outside and lined with a sleeve.

    Why it matters The outward slope stops water running back into the wall.

  3. Mounted level on rated brackets with room for airflow and service, on anti-vibration pads.

    Why it matters Leave space in front of the fan and around the coil for hot air to escape.

  4. Two insulated copper lines — liquid and gas — flared and tightened onto the service valves.

    Why it matters Correct flaring and tightening prevent slow gas leaks.

  5. The interconnect cable runs to the outdoor terminal block on a dedicated, properly earthed supply.

    Why it matters Use the cable size and breaker rated for your AC.

  6. Routed with a continuous downward slope to a safe drain point, never upward.

    Why it matters Pouring water into the tray before finishing confirms it drains properly.

  7. Lines are vacuumed and leak-tested before the valves open; the wall hole is sealed and pipes taped neatly.

    Why it matters Removing air and moisture protects the compressor and keeps cooling efficient.

How an Air Conditioner Cools Your Room

Cooling means moving heat from your room to the outside air. Blue arrows show cool air; orange arrows show heat leaving.

  1. The indoor fan pulls warm air in through the top grille.

  2. Mesh filters trap dust before the air reaches the coil.

  3. Refrigerant inside the coil evaporates and absorbs heat, so the air leaving the coil is cooler and drier.

  4. The cross-flow blower and louver spread cool air evenly across the room.

  5. The compressor draws the refrigerant, now carrying the room's heat, to the outdoor unit and compresses it.

  6. The outdoor fan blows air across the condenser coil and the heat leaves with the warm air. The cooled refrigerant then returns indoors.
